text: "Hacker" is a vague, unhelpful word. Security teams instead think in categories of threat actor, because the category tells you a lot about motivation, skill level, and resources — which tells you what defenses actually matter. Today we'll walk through the five major categories, compare how they differ, and then look at the attack surface they're all going after and why shrinking it works.

A nation-state actor works for a government and wants espionage, intellectual property theft, or disruption — highly sophisticated and well-resourced, sometimes spending years on one target, which is why they're linked to advanced persistent threats. Organized crime is purely financially motivated — ransomware, fraud, business email compromise — sophisticated and well-funded, but running crime as a business rather than chasing a strategic target. A hacktivist is driven by ideology, using defacement or leaks to make a statement, with sophistication varying widely. An insider threat already has legitimate access, making them hard to catch with perimeter defenses. A script kiddie has low skill and resources, running tools someone else built.

Lined up side by side, the differences are stark: nation-states and organized crime bring real sophistication and real resources, hacktivists vary wildly, and script kiddies bring almost none of either — but insiders don't need sophistication at all, because they're already on the inside.

Your attack surface is every point where an attacker could potentially get in — every internet-facing server, every API endpoint, every open port and cloud storage bucket, every vendor with access to your network, and every employee who can be phished. It's almost always bigger than people assume, because it includes things that aren't obviously IT, like a forgotten test server nobody remembered was still running.

A smaller attack surface means fewer things to monitor and fewer things an attacker can try. That looks like decommissioning forgotten servers, disabling unused services and ports, enforcing least privilege so a compromised account can't reach everything, and patching known vulnerabilities before they're exploited.

None of that stops a determined nation-state actor on its own, but it removes the easy wins that organized crime and script kiddies rely on, which is most of the actual traffic a defender deals with. Next lesson: how a vulnerability, a threat, and risk relate — and why risk, not vulnerability count, is what actually drives prioritization.
